tldr: Lauwers argues that APIs are becoming a primary interface and shows, with a postage-pricing example, how explicit data, meaning, machine-readable errors and next actions let agents act safely.
summary: Lauwers, a long-time Devoxx steering committee member speaking for the first time, starts from a claim by Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince that bot traffic now exceeds human HTTP requests. Workflow knowledge has long been trapped in UIs: which button is enabled, what an error means, what comes next. An agent calling the API gets none of that. His example is a bpost chatbot reported in April that could not say what a stamp costs, then declared it was glad to have helped. Putting a chatbot in front of a system does not make it AI-ready; the agent needs a trusted capability such as 'calculate the price of a shipment'.

He then evolves one endpoint. A bad version takes cryptic parameters (type, w, d) and returns a bare string; a good one returns product code, amount, currency and validity date; an AI-first one adds meaning (why the shipment qualifies) and available actions such as buying postage. Errors carry a stable code, the missing inputs and the action they unlock, close to HATEOAS, he admits. Valid values come inline when few, or via a schema or reference-data endpoint when many. 'MCP around a bad API is still a bad API.' Agents get only the user's delegated permissions, purchases need explicit confirmation, and the domain, never the model, sets the price.
keyPoints: An AI-first API response has three layers: data, meaning (why this result and which rules applied) and the next valid actions.
Errors should carry a stable code, the missing fields, why they are needed and the action that becomes possible, so the agent can ask the user a precise follow-up question instead of guessing.
Return allowed values directly only for small, stable sets; for large or changing ones such as country codes, reference a schema or a reference-data endpoint in the API description.
Wrapping a poorly designed API in an MCP server does not fix hidden workflows, vague errors or unsafe write operations.

Agents act with the user's delegated permissions, not as super users; state-changing actions should be marked as requiring confirmation and every tool call logged with inputs, outcome and a correlation ID.
takeaways: Audit one endpoint: replace cryptic parameter names and string responses with explicit fields, units and currency.
Make error responses machine-readable with stable codes and a list of missing or invalid inputs.
Expose the next allowed actions, and whether they need user confirmation, in the response instead of only in UI logic or documentation.
Log agent tool calls with correlation IDs so you can audit what an agent did in your system.

quotes.text: MCP around a bad API is still a bad API.
AI does not get permissions because it's intelligent, it gets exactly the permissions delegated by the user.
An AI-first API does not let AI make your business decisions. It makes your business capabilities explicit enough for AI to use them safely.

watchIf: You own a business API and want a concrete checklist for making its responses and errors usable by AI agents without letting the model make business decisions.
